items.message: AST-walk of files under `root` follows symlinks via `rglob`. A pack whose distribution root contains a symlink pointing outside its own tree (e.g. to `/etc/passwd` or to a site-packages module with executable code) would be walked and its content parsed. The practical consequence is two-fold: (1) the `imports()` result could be forced to `modules` or `unknown` by a crafted symlink in a distribution an attacker controls, and (2) `path.read_text()` on an attacker-placed symlink reads an arbitrary …[truncated]

Path traversal in `_module_root`: `dist.locate_file(recorded)` is called for every path in `dist.files` whose first component matches the top-level module name. `recorded` comes from distribution metadata, which an attacker-controlled distribution can set to any value including `../../outside`. The result is `.resolve()`d, which follows symlinks and canonicalises, but the resolved path is then returned directly as the pack's `root`. Downstream callers (`read`, `file`, `corpus`, `cassettes`) join…[truncated]

Arbitrary module import via `importlib.import_module(module_name)` where `module_name` is taken verbatim from the entry-point value of an installed distribution (`Pack.module`). Entry-point values in a distribution's metadata are attacker-controlled for any distribution an attacker can cause to be installed. The import runs the module's top-level code unconditionally. This is only reached when `imports()` returned `'modules'` and `load=True`, so the AST check is a gate, but the gate only checks …[truncated]

In `guardrails()`, `self.read(f'prompts/{name}.md')` constructs a path by interpolating the caller-supplied `name` directly. A `name` of `../../lockstep` would resolve to `self.root / 'prompts/../../lockstep.md'`, i.e. `self.root / 'lockstep.md'` — outside the `prompts/` subdirectory.
